documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. Findings The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. Research limitations/implications This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. Practical implications The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. Social implications By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. Originality/value This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

Abstract This study investigates how artificial intelligence tools improve perceived innovation capability within sports firms, focusing on the parallel mediating roles of workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, and the moderating role of perceived digital transformation climate. Drawing on Social Identity Theory and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, we argue that AI functions as a vital organizational resource, triggering three parallel pathways toward innovation: affective, identity-based, and motivational. We collected survey data from 611 employees of Chinese sports enterprises and analyzed the data using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results reveal that AI significantly enhances perceived innovation capability directly and indirectly through workplace enjoyment and supportive climate, organizational identification, and AI-enhanced work engagement, among which organizational identification showed the largest indirect point estimate, though pairwise contrasts were not statistically significant. In addition, perceived digital transformation climate positively moderates the direct association between artificial intelligence tools and perceived innovation capability. These findings provide an integrated framework for unpacking AI-enabled innovation in sports organizations, emphasizing the importance of employees’ workplace experience and strategic perceived digital transformation climate. Theoretical contributions and practical managerial implications for sports-sector digital innovation are discussed.

Online research platforms underpin much of what science claims about people, on the assumption that a human produced each response. Generative AI threatens that assumption by letting participants delegate responses to a chatbot, yet how often they do so remains unclear because prior estimates rely on self-report or automated detection rather than direct observation. We surveyed 2,500 workers on a high quality online research platform and directly observed AI assistance by linking donated ChatGPT histories to platform submission records of weekly ChatGPT users, covering 712,930 submissions across more than 127,000 studies. Although one in eight surveyed workers reported ever using AI on a study and 68% of observed workers had done so, assistance appeared in only 1% of submissions, with no detectable increase over more than 3 years. Assistance was often temporally localized within tasks and highly concentrated among workers, with 5% accounting for 64% of assisted submissions. Where assistance occurred, workers were virtually always paid, even when study instructions prohibited AI use, with overall approval rates similar to those for unassisted submissions. Half of assisted submissions involved bounded responses, outside the scope of the platform's LLM detector for open-ended responses. Taken together, our results do not support the view that AI assistance currently poses an existential threat to online research, but reveal limited payment consequences for prohibited use and gaps in platform safeguards, leaving platforms poorly prepared should that threat materialize.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence in scientific writing and mathematical formalization creates a corresponding need for review methods capable of validating rapidly generated, multidisciplinary technical work. We present and retrospectively evaluate an AI-augmented peer-review architecture in which distinct review stages are assigned orthogonal objectives: mathematical correctness, concordance with an established formal framework, chemical admissibility of molecular claims, targeted verification of revisions, and final meta-review. The method is examined through the development of The Chrysene Formalism Revisited: A Twelve-Axiom Foundation for Molecular Characterization, Tensorial Noncommutative Geometry, and Operator Response, a manuscript whose mathematical development is externally constrained by a molecular reference structure. The complete review trajectory was reconstructed as a coded revision ledger. Sixty-four review/process actions were identified, of which 63 were manuscript-directed. Twenty-two revisions (34.9%) were classified as major, 20 (31.7%) as structural, and 59 (93.7%) were fully adopted. Forty-eight actions (76.2%) were explicitly verified in a subsequent review cycle, increasing to 55 (87.3%) when indirect later verification was included. The review disciplines generated markedly different correction profiles. Mathematics produced 35 of the 63 manuscript-directed actions and accounted for all coded proof/analytic repairs and theorem-strength corrections. Concordance generated nine actions, all of which were major and structural, including every action classified as structural restoration. Chemistry generated eight actions concentrated primarily in molecular qualification and nomenclature. The pivotal event was the failure of a mathematically improved manuscript to pass concordance review, requiring substantial reconstruction before renewed chemistry and mathematics review. The case therefore suggests that the value of AI augmentation may lie not simply in increasing review volume, but in separating validation objectives, preserving reviewer disagreement as diagnostic information, distinguishing criticism from revision and verification, and maintaining an auditable record of manuscript development. Because this is a single retrospective case study without a conventional peer-review control group, the results do not establish the superiority of AI-augmented review. They instead provide a reproducible framework for prospective evaluation across future manuscripts.

This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) affects academic deviance among criminology students at the University of the Visayas. Using a quantitative research design, it gathered data from 278 randomly selected respondents to assess how AI tools affect students’ study habits, academic integrity, and ethical decision-making. The results show that AI can make learning more efficient and effective, but it also brings risks such as academic dishonesty, overreliance on technology, and reduced independent thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. ChatGPT is the AI tool respondents use most often, showing that conversational AI is becoming more popular in academic settings. The study also finds that students with some experience using AI understand its benefits and challenges, but they do not have advanced skills or a strong understanding of ethics. Gender and year level play important roles in how students use AI. Even though institutions try to encourage ethical use of AI, there is still a gap between what policies say and what actually happens. The study suggests adding AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and monitoring systems to academic programs. This approach supports responsible AI use, protects academic integrity, and helps future criminology professionals think independently. These findings are meant to guide educational strategies and policies as digital learning becomes more common.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The cost of study abroad has been a barrier to access for a greater number of students. As a high-impact program, alternative access to study abroad should be pressing. Literature considers study abroad and artificial intelligence in isolation of each other; indicating a deeper widening research gap challenging artificial intelligence as not adequately fitted for alternate resource. Review methodology were limited to high-quality academic research databases. The findings revealed that AI has the capacity to expand access to study abroad through state agency support for institutions, and personalized learning. Access can be enhanced when institutions reverse from operating AI as an isolation, but as exploration of study abroad. Advancing AI supported study abroad programs requires greater investment in technological infrastructure and resources.

Automatic Short Answer Scoring (ASAS) is central to NLP for Education. However, openly available benchmarks remain scarce, and existing datasets largely address how well students answer a question directly rather than how well they master underlying concepts (knowledge elements) such as thermal energy or epistemic activities (skills) such as reasoning or claim. To address this gap, we introduce Alice, a large-scale, rubric-based German ASAS dataset that is pedagogically aligned and comprises three subtasks: (i) learning performance (Alice-LP), (ii) knowledge elements (Alice-KE), and (iii) skills (Alice-SK). We further formulate rubric-based ASAS as a rubric-retrieval task and benchmark the dataset with a range of language models, from encoder-only models to lightweight LLMs. We also benchmark the dataset with zero-shot prompting via LLMs and a standard classification baseline. The experiments show that LLMs, in particular, struggle to score knowledge elements and skills in the zero-shot setting. They also indicate that rubric text is often useful, especially for Alice-KE and Alice-SK, while on Alice-LP gains over sample-solution-focused inputs are more modest and vary by model and input format.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is widely commemorated through symbolic rituals, yet his radical paradigm of social justice remains underutilised as a critical framework for contemporary structural challenges. In 2026 India, rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), automated decision-making, and digital public infrastructure (DPI) have transformed socio-political and economic relations. However, stark disparities in digital infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and literacy have codified new, technocratic layers of inequality that deeply impact India's Gen Z demographic. This study examines technological inequality through a structural reinterpretation of Ambedkar’s philosophy of social justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. Utilising an analytical evaluation of institutional datasets spanning 2018-2025, we map rural-urban divides, pedagogical gaps, economic asymmetries in enterprise and agriculture, and localised algorithmic biases. The article argues that inclusive, democratised technological governance is not merely a policy preference but a constitutional imperative required to preserve human dignity in an increasingly automated state. Keywords: Ambedkar; Artificial Intelligence; Digital Equality; Gen Z; Social Justice; India
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Lower back pain (LBP) is prevalent among nursing staff in long-term care facilities. This condition has been linked to repetitive resident handling, sustained non-neutral postures, and cumulative physical workloads. Despite growing interest in exoskeletons as ergonomic and digital assistive technologies (DAT), evidence regarding the implementation of active exoskeletons in real-world nursing practice remains limited. Objective The objective of this exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study was to evaluate the implementation of the HAL® Lumbar Type active exoskeleton in long-term care settings. Specifically, this study explored feasibility, usability, nurses’ acceptance, and descriptive pain-related outcomes under real-world conditions. Methods A non-randomized exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study was conducted in three long-term residential care facilities in Germany. The HAL® Lumbar Type was introduced for use in routine nursing practice during a 90-day intervention period. Objective utilization and adherence data were not systematically recorded. Quantitative outcomes ( n = 15) included subjective LBP, functional impairment, and health-related quality of life measured using the visual analog scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and 8-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-8), respectively. A qualitative semi-structured interview study ( n = 9) explored participants’ experiences of usability, workflow integration, and acceptance. Qualitative data were analyzed using systematic text condensation. Results The findings suggested a pattern of ambivalent acceptance. Caregivers reported situational support during forward-leaning and transfer-related activities, particularly through perceived postural stabilization. The aggregated unpaired VAS data showed no descriptive group-level reduction in subjective pain, and individual pain trajectories could not be assessed. Some participants had lower ODI scores at follow-up, whereas the SF-8 trajectories were heterogeneous and partially indicated a lower health-related quality of life. Participants described spatial limitations, device weight, thermal discomfort, restricted mobility, and the time required for donning and adjustment as barriers to routine use. Participants reported using the exoskeleton selectively for specific high-load tasks rather than continuously throughout shifts. Conclusion The active lumbar exoskeleton was perceived to provide task-specific ergonomic or postural support during selected physical care activities. However, participants’ accounts suggested that the perceived practical viability of the device and their willingness to use it may be associated with workflow compatibility, ease of use, perceived fit, and organizational conditions. Long-term adoption beyond the intervention period was not assessed. Future advancements in exoskeleton technology should prioritize lightweight designs, customized fits, and seamless integration strategies into dynamic nursing workflows. Larger longitudinal studies with appropriate comparison groups and objective biomechanical measures are needed to determine the clinical effectiveness and further examine implementation conditions in nursing practice.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Accurate evaluation is central to selecting which LLM to deploy, yet testing a candidate on live traffic exposes real users to an unvetted model. Teams therefore evaluate candidates offline, on data produced by already-deployed models. This is off-policy evaluation (OPE), and it faces two distribution shifts: as a model is updated in post-training, its responses diverge from the logged ones (policy shift), and the reward definition under which it is judged changes with business requirements (reward shift). Classical OPE methods are ill-suited to this continual-deployment setting because they are defined per task and require fitting from scratch on every new logged dataset or reward definition. To address this, we propose PFN-OPE, a prior-data fitted network that amortizes OPE across a distribution of contextual-bandit tasks. We pretrain it once on tasks constructed from a pool of LLM responses scored by several reward functions, in which both shifts occur. At test-time it maps a logged dataset and one sampled target response per prompt to a value estimate in a single forward pass, with no per-task fitting. On HelpSteer2 and UltraFeedback with Qwen, Llama, and Gemma policies, PFN-OPE achieves 2.0 to 9.3 times lower error than the best baselines across all tested configurations in the reward-shifted settings.

The purpose of this chapter is to analyse the Safe System in road safety as it is related to the topic addressed in this handbook: how to apply an understanding of human factors to the design and management of roads. Road safety is a complex system; by looking at the elements of the Safe System, it is concluded that it oversimplifies both the scope of road safety and the tasks required to significantly reduce road trauma. An assessment of the Safe System against the previous “traditional” approach concludes that an understanding of cognitive human factors (as they relate to road design and traffic management) plays no part in the Safe System, which focuses primarily (though not exclusively) on reducing the consequences of crashes, nor is seeking to address the causes of crashes a part of it. The Safe System regards human error as inevitable, which leaves no scope for road designs and traffic management techniques to be adjusted to avoid errors that lead to crashes. As many practitioners still seek to prevent crashes from happening, it is concluded that they are applying a hybrid of the traditional approach and the Safe System.

Decisions that will shape future fusion facilities, including the production of waste, the management of tritium, the achievement of safety, and impacts on land, water, and local communities, are increasingly becoming sociotechnical in nature. For prior energy technologies, fission among them, such decisions were made top-down and met sustained public opposition. Research shows such opposition is rarely a deficit of public understanding and is instead rooted in place-specific environmental, health, sociocultural, and economic concerns and in distrust of how technologies are selected and sited. We argue that fusion developers have an opportunity to design differently, and we propose an ecology of participation: multiple, complementary modalities of engagement sustained over time, replacing the one-off public consultations now typical of large infrastructure projects. We synthesize human- and environment-centered design frameworks and introduce a framework that reinterprets opposition as a divergence between communities and technology developers in values, norms, or design characteristics. We present six case studies from our work: participatory technology assessment focus groups, participatory design workshops, immersive virtual-reality models of a fusion facility, the Global Fusion Forum platform, the Imaginary Energies speculative design platform, and Heartbeat, an arts-based sound installation. Mapping these onto the values-norms-design framework shows how each interrogates or closes a different part of the expert-public gap, and exposes two limitations of fusion public engagement efforts writ large: developers are seldom asked to articulate their own values and norms, and the environment is represented only indirectly. We close with five guiding questions for fusion researchers building their own participatory engagements.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

documents.abstract: Automated resume screening and Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) increasingly incorporate machine learning components and neural language models. While deep learning methods can capture complex linguistic patterns, their computational overhead, potential opacity, and sensitivity to unvetted training distributions pose practical and ethical challenges for lightweight, transparent academic deployments. In this paper, we describe an open, lightweight, and explainable resume–job description matching system that couples deterministic rule-based information extraction with optional Large Language Model (LLM) qualitative feedback. The core pipeline processes PDF, DOCX, and plain-text resumes, detects functional sections, extracts technical competencies using an auditable 108-skill taxonomy, and evaluates resume–job description compatibility using explicit set operations and a bounded 100-point heuristic score covering Skills, Experience, Projects, Education, and Certifications. To benchmark the pipeline without making real-world recruitment claims, we developed a deterministic synthetic evaluation harness containing 100 resumes, 20 job descriptions, 320 evaluation pairs, and 20 candidate ranking cohorts. Under the synthetic benchmark, the system achieved F1-scores of 0.791 for skill extraction, 0.827 for education, 0.772 for experience, 0.759 for projects, and 0.865 for missing-skill identification. Robustness testing exposed 0.0% recall when experience titles and dates were separated across lines and complete section collapse under unsupported headings. Synonym normalization increased skill recall from 0.896 to 0.968 under controlled conditions. The results characterize the behavior and limitations of the proposed deterministic baseline and provide a reproducible basis for future evaluation with real, anonymized and human-annotated resume data. The benchmark also reports multi-format consistency and controlled baseline comparisons to expose formatting sensitivity and vocabulary-related error patterns.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in second language (L2) learning, yet the cognitive demands of AI-mediated environments, particularly for logographic languages such as Chinese, remain underexplored. This study investigated the interrelationships among executive function (EF), reading-related linguistic skills, AI literacy, and Chinese L2 reading comprehension in 155 Form 4 Southeast Asian ethnic minority students in Hong Kong. Using a quantitative design, we validated a three-factor EF model (working memory, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control) and examined how these components, together with orthographic and morphological skills, relate to L2 reading outcomes. Structural equation modeling showed that all three EF components significantly predicted reading comprehension, underscoring the importance of executive control for processing a complex logographic script. AI literacy significantly supported both foundational reading skills and overall reading comprehension. A key finding of the integrated model is that cognitive flexibility significantly predicted AI literacy, which in turn significantly predicted reading comprehension, indicating an indirect pathway from EF to reading via AI literacy. This pattern highlights the cognitive underpinnings of digital engagement in L2 learning. The study extends the Reading Systems Framework by positioning AI literacy as an external scaffold that interacts with learners’ cognitive resources, and offers practical implications for designing cognitively supportive, AI-enhanced Chinese L2 instruction for ethnic minority learners.

The growing prevalence of mental health challenges has accelerated the adoption of AI-powered mental health care platforms (such as, “wysa”, “ChatGPT Health”), offering scalable, accessible, and personalized support. While initial adoption has been explored, limited research has addressed the factors influencing users’ continued engagement with these platforms. This study investigates both facilitators and barriers that shape users’ sustained use of AI-powered mental health services. By integrating theoretical perspectives from the “Theory of Consumption Values”, and “Status Quo Bias theory”, we formulated a conceptual model addressing cognitive, emotional, and behavioral components. This model was empirically validated using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with data collected from 502 respondents in Bangladesh. The findings reveal that platform quality, expediency value, social value, conditional value, and epistemic value significantly promote continuance intention. Conversely, perceived inertia, perceived threat, and regret avoidance significantly hinder continued use. These insights offer critical implications for designers, developers, and policymakers aiming to enhance user retention and mental health outcomes through AI-powered care solutions.

Objective This study integrates the Delphi method with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to identify, refine, and prioritize occupational health risk factors in the petroleum and petrochemical industry. The aim is to construct a transparent sector-specific indicator hierarchy for decision support where complete and comparable plant-level data are not yet available. Methods Twenty purposively selected experts completed two Delphi rounds. Importance was rated on a five-point scale and summarized using the mean and coefficient of variation (CV); qualitative comments were used to address conceptual overlap, measurability, and privacy concerns. Expert authority was calculated as Cr = (Ca + Cs)/2. After the indicator hierarchy was finalized, six senior experts from the original panel completed AHP pairwise comparisons. Priority weights and consistency ratios (CR) were calculated, with CR < 0.10 regarded as acceptable internal consistency. Results All 20 experts completed both Delphi rounds. The mean expert authority coefficient was 0.813 (range 0.70–0.91). Four first-level and twelve second-level indicators were retained. Process safety risk received the highest first-level weight, followed by work environment risk, occupational behavior risk, and individual health status risk. Primary containment failure, physical hazards, and safety-system performance received the largest overall indicator weights. All AHP judgment matrices met the CR < 0.10 consistency criterion. Conclusion The Delphi-AHP framework provides an expert-derived structure for prioritizing occupational health risks and linking them to site-level management actions. The weights are decision-support priorities rather than validated predictors of occupational illness or accidents. External validation with plant-level exposure, incident, and health-outcome data is required before broad regulatory or cross-company application.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study investigates the factors influencing aviation incident outcomes, with a focus on distinguishing between crash events and emergency landings. A curated dataset of 53 aviation incidents was analyzed using logistic regression and machine learning classifiers to identify the most influential human, technical, and operational variables. The analysis adopts a sociotechnical framework, examining how interactions between human performance and engineering design contribute to incident severity. Statistical results indicate that human factor variables and issues are the predictors exhibiting significant differences between crash and noncrash outcomes, with human factors demonstrating the strongest association. Chi-square analysis further confirms the significance of human factors ([Formula: see text]), while multicollinearity diagnostics (variance inflation factor [VIF] ≈ 2) support model stability. Among machine learning models, the support vector machine achieved the highest predictive accuracy (91%), indicating that aviation incident outcomes exhibit structured and separable patterns within the feature space. The findings emphasize that adverse outcomes are more strongly associated with deficiencies in training, communication, and situational awareness than with isolated technical faults. The study concludes that integrating human factors analysis and predictive modeling into the system development lifecycle can enable proactive risk identification and enhance aviation safety.

General Background Occupational health and safety management serves as a critical foundation for operational continuity and workforce protection in industrial logistics environments. Specific Background In spare part transit warehouses, manual handling and material logistics frequently present severe physical hazards to warehouse personnel. Knowledge Gap Although hazard evaluation tools are widely recognized, systematic evaluations focusing on spare part transit hub operational workflows remain insufficiently documented. Aims This study evaluates occupational safety risks and formulates targeted risk mitigation strategies within a transit warehouse setting. Results Evaluating 22 identified operational hazard risks via the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Risk Control framework revealed 18 low-risk occurrences and 4 moderate-risk conditions, primarily involving respiratory discomfort, cut injuries, muscle strain, and hand pinching during spare part handling. Novelty A targeted risk control framework specifically tailored to spare part transit logistics operations is established. Implications Implementing structured engineering controls, administrative protocols, and personal protective equipment provides a practical blueprint to minimize workplace accidents and improve operational safety compliance in logistics transit facilities. Key Findings Highlights Operational hazard evaluation across transit warehouse activities identified 22 potential risk points, with 18 categorized as low risk and 4 as moderate risk. Moderate-risk hazards primarily stem from manual spare part handling, leading to respiratory issues, physical cuts, muscle strain, and pinching injuries. Mitigation strategies combining engineering modifications, administrative procedures, and proper safety equipment effectively diminish operational workplace hazards. Keywords Risk Control, HIRARC, Occupational Health And Safety, Transit Warehouse, Hazard Identification
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Robots operating in dynamic environments require reliable detection of how their surroundings change over time. Existing learning-based methods largely rely on pairwise 2D image features, which struggle under large viewpoint changes and occlusions, are sensitive to noise, and show limited generalization across domains, while explicit 3D approaches typically require costly offline optimization. We show that the implicit 3D knowledge of Geometric Foundation Models (GFMs) provides a strong basis for addressing these limitations. We introduce Argos, which adapts GFM features for joint scene change detection and 3D reconstruction. To address data scarcity and take a step toward a foundation model for scene change detection, we introduce a large-scale benchmark comprising two synthetic datasets and one real-world dataset, and train jointly across diverse datasets to improve cross-domain generalization. We further introduce Argos-SLAM, a real-time system designed for robotics, which performs online change detection and change-aware 4D mapping. Across benchmarks, our framework substantially outperforms existing baselines, with gains of up to 42.01% in change IoU and 27.91% in F1, while supporting scalable deployment in changing real-world environments.

Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries remains at nascent stages, particularly in developing economies. Understanding librarians' adoption patterns, institutional readiness, and perceived opportunities and challenges is crucial for strategic planning. Purpose: This study examines the level and extent of AI adoption in academic libraries, identifies key AI applications, explores perceived opportunities and challenges, and assesses librarians' readiness for AI integration. Method: A quantitative descriptive survey design was employed. The study population comprised librarians and library professionals from 15 academic libraries across Nigeria's North-East geopolitical zone (n = 127, 89.4% response rate). Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with eight sections (Likert-scale items, Section A–H) and analysed using descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation) and inferential statistics (Pearson correlation, independent t-tests, one-way ANOVA). Instrument validity was established through expert validation and content validity index (CVI = 0.89); reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's alpha (α = 0.81). Results: Current AI adoption rates remain low (mean = 2.34/5.0), with limited AI applications in catalogue management (mean = 2.41/5.0) and reference services (mean = 1.98/5.0). Significant positive correlations emerged between librarians' AI skills and adoption willingness (r = 0.67, p < 0.001) and between institutional support and adoption rates (r = 0.58, p < 0.001). Major opportunities identified include enhanced information retrieval (mean = 4.23/5.0) and improved user experience (mean = 4.18/5.0); critical challenges included inadequate infrastructure (mean = 4.41/5.0), limited funding (mean = 4.37/5.0), and insufficient AI skills (mean = 4.29/5.0). Conclusion: Strategic institutional investment, targeted capacity-building programmes, and supportive institutional policies are essential to accelerate AI adoption. Recommendations prioritise AI literacy training for librarians, infrastructure development, institutional AI frameworks, and collaboration between academic libraries and technology partners. These findings contribute evidence-based insights for policymakers, university management, and LIS educators navigating AI integration in academic library environments.

topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education, healthcare, child protection, and social protection across Africa presents both transformative opportunities and serious structural risks to the realisation of children’s rights. This chapter argues that navigating this terrain requires more than the uncritical adoption of externally designed governance frameworks. It demands engagement with the normative architecture of African children’s rights law, anchored in the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC), and with the Human Rights-Based Approach (HRBA) as both a conceptual and operational framework to ensure that AI serves children as rights-holders rather than as data subjects. Drawing on African philosophical traditions, particularly Ubuntu , the emerging continental policy architecture of the African Union, and country-level evidence from across the continent, the chapter advances a child-centred, African-rooted normative framework for AI governance that speaks from African experience to global debates. It does so not as a regional adaptation of Northern models, but as an independent normative contribution. It contends that realising children’s rights through AI is not a technical problem but a challenge of justice that requires political will, institutional innovation, and the sustained centring of Africa’s children in decisions that will shape their lives.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
keywords: African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child

documents.abstract: Objectives. Smart technologies of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), have significant potential to enhance occupational health and safety programs. This scoping review examines AI applications in personal protective equipment (PPE). Methods. Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework, PubMed, Web of Science and Google Scholar were systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2024. Two independent reviewers screened 277 records, and 47 studies met the inclusion criteria. Results. AI applications in PPE were categorized into three domains: AI-based PPE compliance detection (59.6%) using computer vision and deep learning for automated monitoring of helmets, masks and vests; big data-driven PPE stockpiling and analysis frameworks (17.0%) for supply chain management and inventory optimization; and AI-based smart PPE for occupational hazard prevention (23.4%) integrating sensors and AI algorithms for real-time worker monitoring and risk prediction. The most commonly employed techniques included convolutional neural networks, YOLO, SSD and support vector machines, with applications across construction, healthcare, oil and gas, and nuclear industries. Conclusion. Integration of AI with PPE has demonstrated promising results in enhancing worker safety across various industries. This emerging field requires further research attention and wider industrial implementation to fully realize its potential in preventing occupational injuries and illnesses.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies is transforming the accounting and financial reporting environment. Traditional accounting processes increasingly rely on automated data processing, machine learning, intelligent document recognition, predictive analytics, and digital financial reporting systems. These technologies create opportunities to improve the efficiency, accuracy, transparency, and timeliness of accounting information. At the same time, the adoption of AI introduces new challenges related to data quality, cybersecurity, professional competence, ethical responsibility, explainability, and regulatory oversight. This study examines the opportunities and challenges associated with the application of artificial intelligence in accounting, with particular attention to emerging economies. The research applies a qualitative review-based methodology and analyses academic literature, professional publications, and international developments in digital financial reporting. The findings indicate that AI can significantly reduce repetitive accounting tasks, support financial analysis, improve fraud detection, and enhance the accessibility of financial information. However, technological adoption alone does not guarantee high- high-quality accounting outcomes. The effectiveness of AI depends on data quality, appropriate governance mechanisms, professional judgement, digital skills, and institutional readiness. The study argues that emerging economies should adopt a balanced human–AI approach in which artificial intelligence supports, rather than replaces, professional accounting judgement. The paper concludes by proposing key directions for responsible AI adoption in accounting, including professional education, data governance, cybersecurity, regulatory development, and continuous human oversight. Keywords: artificial intelligence; accounting; digital transformation; financial reporting; emerging economies; machine learning; accounting information systems; professional judgement

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an enterprise-level capability rather than a stand-alone technology, but firms differ substantially in their ability to convert AI resources into sustained innovation performance. This study proposes a conditional process model in which AI capability enhances enterprise innovation performance through knowledge sharing, while environmental dynamism strengthens the innovation value of shared knowledge. Building on the resource-based view, the knowledge-based view, and contingency theory, AI capability is conceptualized as the organizational ability to mobilize AI-relevant data, technologies, human expertise, coordination routines, and change capacity. Knowledge sharing is expected to transmit the effects of AI capability by increasing the circulation and recombination of data-driven insights across organizational units. Environmental dynamism is positioned as a second-stage moderator because rapidly changing markets and technologies increase the value of timely knowledge recombination for innovation. A two-wave managerial survey is proposed for Chinese high-tech, digital-service, and advanced-manufacturing enterprises. IBM SPSS Statistics and Hayes' PROCESS Macro provide the core analytical environment. The design combines reliability tests, exploratory factor analysis, common-method diagnostics, correlation analysis, hierarchical regression, and PROCESS Model 14 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. The manuscript provides a publication-oriented theoretical argument, an adaptable questionnaire, SPSS syntax, and results tables that can be populated with actual data after collection.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cross-border artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation is expanding, but evidence on its effect on domestic technological capability in recipient economies is scarce. Drawing on absorptive capacity theory, we create a composite AI absorptive capacity index for 10 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) economies, encompassing innovation foundations, application foundations and industrial support. We measure bilateral AI cooperation intensity via co-publications, co-patents and investment linkages. Using a 2015-2025 bilateral panel with fixed-effects and three-way fixed-effects models, we find a positive association between cooperation intensity and absorptive capacity, robust across all three index dimensions and to sample restrictions and winsorization. Heterogeneity analysis shows that China-related cooperation offers no general premium. A more favourable link emerges only in economies with weaker initial industrial foundations, and it is fragile under stricter sample restrictions. The findings imply that the developmental value of AI cooperation hinges not on cooperation volume but on embedding external knowledge into domestic learning, application and industrial adaptation systems.

Manual data entry and curation is the most used method of data collection for real world evidence and clinical trials but is a time-consuming task associated with significant human effort and transcription mistakes. MIRROR is a retrospective study that compared manual data capture from electronic case report forms (eCRF) to automated data extraction from electronic health records (EHRs) using artificial intelligence (AI). Clinical information was extracted from EHRs of 113 breast cancer patients participating in 11 clinical trials, with the system providing references to the original text for each variable to enable efficient verification. All patients were enrolled at the Virgen del Rocío University Hospital (Sevilla, Spain). Analyses provided high rates of accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score for most structured and unstructured clinical data domains. Future efforts should focus on improving unstructured data extraction and implementing standardized eCRF among sites to ensure consistent extraction and evaluation of clinical information.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support literature discovery, manuscript preparation, and evidence synthesis, but effective use depends on practical skills and an understanding of research integrity. This study evaluated participants’ perceptions of an eight-hour, hands-on workshop on AI-assisted academic writing. Methods: A cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation included 64 of 80 registered delegates. The validated questionnaire contained demographic items, Likert-scale statements, nominal-response items, and open-ended questions. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, and qualitative feedback was analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic framework. Results: Before the workshop, 16 participants (25.0%) agreed or strongly agreed that they had a good understanding of AI applications in academic writing, whereas 54 (84.4%) agreed or strongly agreed that their understanding had improved after the workshop. Forty-five participants (70.3%) reported confidence in using AI tools after the workshop, and 44 (68.8%) planned to use them in future academic writing. Qualitative feedback emphasized practical exposure, time-saving applications, and greater awareness of ethical use. Conclusions: Participants reported improved understanding, confidence, and awareness of responsible AI use after the workshop. Structured, practice-oriented AI literacy training may support the responsible integration of AI into academic work, although objective pre-post competency testing is needed in future studies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract In an era defined by digital acceleration, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business decision-making. This chapter explores how AI technologies are reshaping business intelligence, enabling data-driven strategies, and empowering organizations to navigate uncertainty with confidence. From predictive analytics and natural language processing (NLP) to machine learning (ML) models that support real-time decisions, AI stands at the forefront of a paradigm shift toward smarter, agile, and future-proof businesses. This chapter begins with an introduction to the concept of AI-driven decision-making and the critical importance of aligning technological innovation with strategic foresight. It then synthesizes current literature and case studies to illustrate the evolving role of AI in various decision-making contexts. A detailed discussion follows, outlining the organizational strategies and emerging roles necessary to harness AI effectively. The authors then explore key clusters of AI deployment, ranging from finance and marketing to logistics and customer service, and highlight their transformative impact. Finally, this chapter underscores the human dimension, identifying the essential skills and competencies needed to leverage AI responsibly while driving growth. A forward-looking conclusion presents actionable recommendations for integrating AI into long-term decision frameworks, ensuring resilience, ethical alignment, and sustainable business value. This comprehensive narrative offers scholars and practitioners a roadmap for navigating the intersection of AI and strategic decision-making in a rapidly evolving digital landscape.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping language education through automated feedback, speech recognition, adaptive practice, dialogue systems, machine translation, learning analytics, and generative language models. This article critically reviews the principal pedagogical uses of these technologies and examines representative AI-assisted language learning platforms. It adopts an integrative review design that prioritizes peer-reviewed research from established indexed journals, supplemented by international guidance and current platform documentation. The synthesis shows that AI can expand opportunities for repeated practice, individualized feedback, formative assessment, and access to multilingual resources. Evidence is strongest when AI supports a clearly defined task and learners remain responsible for interpreting and revising the output. Important limitations include recognition errors, fabricated or culturally narrow responses, opaque scoring, privacy risks, unequal access, academic-integrity concerns, and excessive dependence on automated correction. A comparison of representative platforms demonstrates that products differ substantially in target skills, feedback, adaptivity, and data demands; they should not be treated as interchangeable. The article proposes a six-stage teacher-guided integration cycle covering learning outcomes, tool selection, accountable interaction, verification, assessment, and impact review. The central conclusion is that effective AI-assisted language education depends less on the novelty of a platform than on pedagogical alignment, human oversight, and learners’ developing capacity to evaluate automated output.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Male factors account for almost half of all infertility cases and afflict approximately 186 million men globally, presenting a substantial and increasing public health burden. Semen analysis is the standard of care for assessing male fertility, but subjective visual interpretation results in > 25–30% inter-observer variability and precludes non-destructive assessment of sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF). Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, has the potential to streamline semen assessment and clinical decision-making throughout male infertility care by providing automated, data-driven approaches that are objective, efficient, and precise. Guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement, the manuscript included research from PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Two independent reviewers screened all retrieved records according to pre-specified inclusion criteria to identify peer-reviewed publications describing applications of machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks, natural language processing, computer vision, and explainable artificial intelligence to semen analysis, fertility status prediction, or assisted reproductive technologies. Artificial Intelligence techniques consistently outperformed conventional semen assessment methods for sperm count, motility, morphology, and predictive analyses. Feedforward Spectral Neural Networks classified sperm concentration with 93% accuracy, while a Fast Region-based Convolutional Neural Network classified sperm motility with 97.37% accuracy; both surpassed inter-observer agreement achievable through WHO-based manual visual analysis. VGG16-pretrained CNNs identified sperm morphology with a true positive rate of 94.1%, however, performance declined substantially to 62% when validated on an independent external dataset. Deep learning models demonstrated the capacity to predict SDF non-destructively, high concordance to TUNEL assay and sperm chromatin structure assay reference standards (r = 0.97, p < 0.001). Machine Learning classifiers specifically, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, and CatBoost, showcased AUCs of 0.998 for the prediction of male fertility status. Furthermore, explainable artificial intelligence techniques such as SHAP and LIME improve the clinical interpretability of machine learning model outputs, an important step toward regulatory acceptance. These techniques can also be integration with computer-assisted sperm analysis systems, smartphone-based semen analysis, sperm sorting for intrauterine insemination, microTESE, ultrasonography, and multi-omics data platforms. Limitations of the current literature include retrospective study designs, single-centre data sources, small sample sizes, lack of external validation, and heterogeneity in image acquisition, outcome measures, and performance metrics. Included studies face challenges relating to algorithmic bias, insufficient model explainability, data security and governance, and the absence of standardized regulation or AI-specific reporting frameworks. Future work should prioritise prospective multicentre studies employing multimodal artificial intelligence that integrates imaging data with genomic, transcriptomic, hormonal, and electronic health record inputs, as well as federated learning and international collaboration to establish standardised and internationally recognised regulatory guidelines. In conclusion, artificial intelligence has the potential to transform clinical decision-making for patients presenting with infertility by enabling objective, high-throughput, and personalised assessment of semen samples. However, these tools should be used to augment rather than replace clinical expertise until models have been prospectively validated across diverse populations and have received appropriate regulatory clearance. Not applicable.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in periodontology marks a revolutionary paradigm for diagnostic verification, therapeutic planning, and general patient care. This review discusses the advent of such automated AI technologies, including machine learning and deep learning models, for periodontal challenges. Highlights include convolutional neural networks (CNNs) being used to detect radiographic bone loss and disease severity and AI-powered modeling to predict treatment outcomes, and educational tools augmenting periodontal training. Practical implications highlight the efficiency, accuracy, price-benefit of AI in clinical settings as well as its potential to be widely implemented in the areas with low accessibility. Although data privacy, variability in methods and ethical concerns are challenges faced by AI, it has huge potential to make progress on precision periodontics. Future directions indicate that AI is to be increasingly integrated with robotics, biomarker studies, and greater global accessibility initiatives, as AI may offer unique solutions to the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of periodontal disease.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Rare diseases collectively affect between 3.5 and 5.9% of the global population. Yet, patients still endure an average diagnostic interval of five to seven years before receiving an accurate explanation of their condition. Approximately 80% of these disorders have a genetic origin, and nearly 95% lack approved disease-modifying therapies that alter the disease course. This combination places enormous pressure on healthcare systems and affected families. In the last decade, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, has emerged as a credible response to these gaps. This narrative review summarizes recent AI contributions across four interrelated dimensions: differential diagnosis and pattern recognition; prognosis and risk stratification; therapeutic discovery and drug repositioning; and the operational organization of rare disease care. Available evidence indicates that AI-based approaches can shorten diagnostic intervals, reduce unnecessary testing, and increase therapeutic options for orphan conditions. Despite these global advances, implementation remains highly unequal. This review foregrounds the Latin American perspective, setting itself apart from broader overviews. The region presents a scenario in which rich genetic diversity and growing collaborative networks coexist with infrastructural bottlenecks and underrepresentation in genomic databases. The integration of AI into rare disease care will depend on federated data infrastructures, transparent and interpretable models, harmonized regulatory frameworks, and sustained investment in workforce training. Patient organizations are essential partners, particularly in emerging economies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Deep learning has made rapid advances in weather forecasting: autoregressive models trained on atmospheric reanalyses now rival dynamical models across nowcasting, medium-range, and subseasonal-to-seasonal lead times, producing well-calibrated ensemble forecasts at reduced cost. We review these advances and consider their extension to climate horizons, where the challenge shifts from initial-condition skill to producing reliable statistical responses under altered forcings. AI-powered climate prediction systems must produce credible forced responses to drivers (e.g., greenhouse gases, land-use change) typically outside the observed record. We propose two minimum requirements for AI in climate modeling: (i) external forcing agents must enter explicitly enough to support interventions in which they vary independently; and (ii) robustness must be stress-tested in out-of-distribution regimes, including extremes and counterfactual trajectories. Using leading AI autoregressive emulators and hybrid physics-AI models, we identify development and coupling challenges. Comparing the reported throughput of these models with that of GPU-ported dynamical models highlights how AI can reduce time-to-solution by advancing only the target variables at the required resolution and using longer time steps, rather than integrating a full high-frequency, multivariate state. Diverse AI downscaling strategies can partially substitute for explicit fine-scale resolution, paving the way toward inexpensive local hazard assessment across prediction horizons.

Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into health professions education, yet evidence on its cognitive and psychological correlates among students in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study examined patterns of AI use and their association with cognitive reflection and psychological well-being among medical and allied health students in Ibadan, Nigeria. Methods An institution-based analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 365 undergraduate medical and allied health students selected through multistage sampling from three tertiary institutions. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire adapted from validated cognitive and psychological assessment instruments. AI-use frequency was the primary exposure, while cognitive reflection and psychological well-being were the primary outcomes. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, analysis of variance, Pearson's correlation, chi-square tests, and multivariable linear regression, adjusting for age, sex, institution, programme of study, and academic level. Results Overall, 92.3% (337/365) of participants reported using AI for academic purposes, with 43.0% using AI daily, and ChatGPT was the predominant platform. AI-use frequency showed a weak positive correlation with cognitive scores (r = 0.120, p = 0.028) and a moderate negative correlation with psychological scores (r=-0.256, p < 0.001). After adjustment for demographic and institutional factors, AI-use frequency remained independently associated with higher cognitive reflection (β = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.23–1.68; p = 0.010) but was not significantly associated with psychological outcomes (β=-0.76, 95% CI: -2.17 to 0.66; p = 0.293). AI use was significantly associated with age (p = 0.047) and institution (p < 0.001), but not gender (p = 0.450). Daily users were also more likely to accept AI-generated responses without verifying their accuracy than occasional users (62.8% vs. 41.8%). Conclusion AI was widely integrated into learning among medical and allied health students and demonstrated a modest independent association with cognitive reflection, whereas psychological outcomes appeared to be more strongly influenced by institutional context than AI use itself. These findings support institution-level AI literacy programmes, governance frameworks, and curricula that promote critical appraisal and responsible AI use in health professions education. documents.abstract: Policy-based reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have produced promising results for autonomous cyber defense; however, they are sample-inefficient in settings where defenders must respond under delayed, partial observations with actions from large action spaces. While large language models (LLMs) may reason semantically about security state space, high latency and trust assumptions prevent attractive in-line deployment models. We introduce Ask the Expert, a training-time guidance framework which first summarizes hard cyber-defense states, then intermittently queries an LLM for host-level defensive recommendations via a constrained action interface, and finally transforms those recommendations into tiered reward shaping for use with PPO. Because the LLM is discarded after training, deployment is a pure RL policy. Across TTCP CAGE CC1 and CC2 and both attacker types, this asymmetric design improves sample efficiency over PPO and outperforms the evaluated potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) baselines, while retaining the strongest terminal mean and requiring no LLM dependency at deployment time.

Large language models (LLMs) can produce inaccurate answers even when relevant facts are supplied in the prompt. This study examines how graph data serialization, entity identifiers, and context selection affect factual question answering in knowledge-augmented prompting. Four synthetic knowledge graph datasets containing 6, 10, 14, and 20 people entities were constructed using the familiar FOAF ontology, which was expanded with custom properties. Eight separate serialization formats were evaluated: natural language, XML, JSON, and RDF/XML and their variants. These formats were combined with two separate LLMs: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Data was supplied through system prompts without training or fine-tuning the models. Three experimental stages examined complete graph contexts, answers obtained using predefined SPARQL queries in AllegroGraph, and descriptions of individual entities. In total, 19,044 model responses were evaluated in the experiment. Results indicate a clear accuracy–complexity trade-off: replacing natural language with XML using full-name identifiers leads to an increase in accuracy, from 54.50% to 89.17% for Llama and from 72.33% to 82.67% for Qwen when considering the 10-person-entity dataset. The findings indicate that optimal LLM reasoning requires a balance between structural rigidity and readability; using explicit, human-readable identifiers instead of numeric abstractions improves context retention and minimizes errors. However, this approach demands caution, as it can lead to up to a 29.72% relative increase in token consumption compared with using natural language. Ultimately, improving LLM information recall requires a carefully calibrated balance between symbolic representation, semantic expressiveness, and knowledge scalability.

documents.abstract: The rapid industrialisation of Sahelian economies exposes a growing population of workers and residents to physical, chemical and radiological risks that remain poorly documented. This article proposes an integrated methodological framework for assessing and monitoring these risks, built around the assess-prevent-monitor-improve loop and a set of six quantitative indicators linking occupational safety and epidemiology. The framework is applied to naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) in extractive industries and to indoor radon, using case studies calibrated on Chadian practice: southern oil fields, a cement plant and a fifteen-building radon survey. Results show that simple measurement tools, a shared risk-rating grid and a strictly applied hierarchy of prevention can bring exposures below international reference levels at costs compatible with the budgets of companies in the subregion. A minimal ten-line dashboard for occupational health services in developing countries is proposed.
